extracted.intended_audience: writers, critics, and educated readers interested in producing or evaluating wit and literary humour
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what counts as 'wit' versus 'false wit' in literary writing (prose and poetry), including tests, permissible devices, and genre-appropriate uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: True Wit (ressemblance of ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit consists in such a resemblance and congruity of ideas as gives Delight and Surprise; it is a joining together of ideas that discovers a congruity not obvious before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True wit arises from a pleasing, surprising congruity of ideas (not merely words). Examples: metaphor, allegory, parable, aenigma, vision, burlesque, and other methods of allusion. The resemblance should not be obvious; it should produce surprize and delight. Locke's account (assemblage of ideas producing pictures in the fancy) is used to explain this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential properties: Delight and Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Every resemblance of ideas only qualifies as wit if it gives the reader 'Delight' and 'Surprise', the latter being particularly essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a purported instance of wit, ask: does it delight? does it surprise? If the likeness is obvious (no surprise), it is not wit. The surprise must come from a congruity that is not immediately evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: False Wit (word-level resemblance and tricks)
rubrics_metrics.description: False wit chiefly consists in the resemblance and congruity of single letters (anagrams, chronograms, lipograms, acrosticks), syllables (echoes, doggerel rhymes), words (puns, quibbles), or whole sentences/poems cast into shapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are mechanical or verbal contrivances that substitute letter/sound-pattern ingenuity for genuine thought. They are often time-consuming, pedantic, and produce little real intellectual pleasure. Examples given: anagrams, acrosticks, chronograms, lipograms, echoes, doggerel, puns, 'poems in the figures of Eggs, Axes, or Altars'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for pun/true wit: translation test
rubrics_metrics.description: The only way therefore to try a Piece of Wit, is to translate it into a different Language: If it bears the Test, you may pronounce it true; but if it vanishes in the Experiment, you may conclude it to have been a Punn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: attempt to render the line/remark in another language; if the effect depends on sound/orthography it will disappear. This distinguishes substantive wit from mere wordplay (pun = 'vox et præterea nihil').

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixt Wit (combination of idea- and word-resemblance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A kind of wit that consists partly in the resemblance of ideas and partly in the resemblance of words; its foundations are partly in truth and partly in falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixt wit can be more or less perfect depending on whether the resemblance lies more in ideas (good) or words (bad). It is most appropriate to epigrams and short occasional pieces; avoid overusing mixt wit in serious or lengthy compositions (Cowley is a cited exemplar; use sparingly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation in Truth and Good Sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The basis of all wit is Truth; no thought can be valuable which is not just and grounded in the nature of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Bouhours' injunction that thoughts must be 'just' and have their foundation in truth. Wit should not be mere cleverness divorced from sense. Evaluate whether the conceit rests on a just relation rather than arbitrary sleight-of-hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety of words and thoughts adapted to the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden's definition: wit as 'a propriety of words and thoughts adapted to the subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison notes this captures good writing generally rather than wit specifically — it is a useful criterion for clarity and aptness (propriety), but not sufficient alone to define wit. Use propriety as part of assessing overall quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / unexpectedness in simile and metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: For a comparison to be witty, the ideas compared must not lie too near each other; obvious similarities give no surprize and thus no wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid banal similes (e.g., 'white as snow') unless an additional surprising twist is added (e.g., 'and as cold too'). The added unexpected element creates wit. When judging metaphors/similies, ask whether they add an unforeseen congruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought over ornament (rhyme and formal tricks)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the thought of a couplet is good, the rhyme adds little; if the thought is bad, the rhyme will not redeem it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devices like 'bouts rimés', double rhymes and doggerel are criticized: do not let contrived rhyme-lists, uncommon rhymes, or technical ingenuity replace substantive thought. Prioritize idea and judgment over ornamental cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriateness of devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain witty devices are suitable only to particular genres: e.g., mixt wit and epigrams are fit subjects for epigrammatic, occasional poetry; heroic/epic poetry aims at greatness and is not the province for such surprises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the wit-device to the genre: avoid puns, acrostics, and other trivial devices in serious, elevated genres; reserve some wordplay for light, occasional, or epigrammatic pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition / antithesis as a legitimate source of wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only resemblance but opposition of ideas often produces wit; turns, antitheses, and contrasts can generate felicitous surprises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider deliberate contrast as a mechanic for producing wit (antithesis, paradox). Evaluate whether the opposition yields a just, surprising insight rather than mere contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical letter/figure contrivances
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices that rely on letter-shapes, numerals, or constrained alphabets (chronograms, acrosticks, lipograms, chronograms) are treated as pedantic, time-consuming, and generally false wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These contrivances may be amusing feats of industry but are often empty of thought; treat them as curiosities, not models for serious wit. They were common in ages of pedantry (e.g., monastic times) but are derided when offered as wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid external mimicry as a mark of wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Some ascribe wit to external mimicry (resembling tone, posture, face); Addison treats this as an overreach — imitation does not equal genuine wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between comic imitation (performance) and literary wit: mere mimicry of manner or sound may produce laughter but is not the same as an intellectual congruity that constitutes true wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance Wit with Judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit (quick assemblage of images and resemblances) is a different faculty from judgment (careful separation of ideas to avoid being misled by similitude); they do not always coexist in the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting or evaluating witty material, ensure it is tempered by judgment: wit should not sacrifice accuracy, clarity, or justness of thought. Be wary of cleverness that confuses or misleads rather than enlightens.
